paper.authors_full: Rosó Baltà-Salvador, Enric Brasó-Vives, Marta Peña
paper.title: Evaluating AI-assisted creative ideation: A crossover study in higher education
paper.pdf_filename: Balta-Salvador Braso-Vives Pena (2026) - Evaluating AI-assisted creative ideation.pdf
paper.version_read: Published version of record, Thinking Skills and Creativity 59 (2026) 101958; DOI 10.1016/j.tsc.2025.101958. Available online 18 August 2025; accepted 16 August 2025 (PDF p. 1).
paper.one_line_finding: Among 51 analyzed students, pooled within-person comparisons found more Existing Solutions with ChatGPT (1.00 vs 0.55, p = .011) and shorter descriptions (23.36 vs 25.57 words, p = .015), with no statistically significant differences in fluency, flexibility, or originality (p. 8, Table 4); thematic diversity was comparable (p. 10, Table 7 and Section 4.3), while semantic divergence was printed as higher with AI (0.29 vs 0.28) despite the narrative describing it as lower (p. 10, Section 4.3).

arms.name: AI-assisted
arms.description: ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) on university computers with internet access limited to ChatGPT. Group B receives AI first; Group A receives AI in the second task. Every participant completes one AI-assisted task.

arms.name: Unaided
arms.description: No computers, external resources, or electronic devices. Group A works unaided first; Group B works unaided after the AI-assisted task. Every participant completes one unaided task.

estimates.question: with_ai
estimates.measure_detail: Methods define average pairwise semantic divergence within each participant's own set of ideas; Results instead call it divergence from the centroid per participant. LaBSE embeddings of descriptions obtained using Gemini OCR with manual checking (PDF p. 7, Section 3.3.2; PDF pp. 10-11, Section 4.3 and Fig. 3).

sources.locator: PDF p. 10, Section 4.3, individual-level semantic divergence
sources.quote: At individual level, the average semantic divergence from the centroid per participant was M= 0.28 (SD = 0.03) for unaided ideas and M= 0.29 (SD = 0.03) for AI-assisted ideas.

sources.locator: PDF p. 10, Section 4.3, paired-samples t-test

estimates.notes: The printed means imply greater divergence with AI, but the abstract, Results interpretation and Discussion describe lower divergence. The t statistic, d, confidence bounds and arm labels are transcribed exactly; no direction has been repaired from the narrative. The confidence-interval target, subtraction order and d standardizer are not identified. Methods describe within-person pairwise distances; Results describe distances from an unspecified centroid per participant. unit and sd_level retain the explicitly described participant level, and within_person retains the stated paired test. However, t(364) is inconsistent with the reported study of 51 people, so analysis-specific participant counts and se_basis remain null. Null se_basis means the implemented independent units are unresolved, not that the paper omitted a test. No participant count is inferred from degrees of freedom, and no values are digitized from Fig. 3.

estimates.outcome: Group-level semantic divergence to the condition centroid
estimates.question: across_people
estimates.measure_detail: Cosine distance of each idea description's LaBSE embedding from the mean embedding of its condition. Both tasks are pooled; text was extracted through Gemini OCR and manually verified (PDF p. 7, Section 3.3.2).

sources.locator: PDF p. 10, Section 4.3, group-level semantic divergence
sources.quote: At group level, the average semantic divergence to the centroid was M= 0.28 (SD = 0.06) for unaided ideas and M= 0.29 (SD = 0.07) for AI-assisted ideas.

sources.locator: PDF p. 10, Section 4.3, independent-samples t-test

estimates.notes: The printed means imply greater divergence with AI, whereas the narrative concludes greater similarity. The signed t, d and confidence bounds are retained exactly as printed. The confidence-interval target, subtraction order and d standardizer are not specified. The independent-samples test analyzes idea-to-condition-centroid distances with no reported participant adjustment; se_basis is output and within_person is null. The same students contribute several ideas and appear in both conditions. n_units is null because the semantic-analysis observation count is not explicitly reported. The separately reported corpus total is 728 ideas (PDF p. 5, Section 3.2.1: "In total, 728 ideas were gathered."); this is descriptive context only, not a confirmed semantic-analysis sample size. The printed t(728) is inconsistent with a conventional independent-samples test on that corpus; the actual semantic-analysis sample and analysis-specific participant counts remain unresolved. Both tasks are pooled. No numbers are digitized from Fig. 3.

open_items: Semantic divergence: the printed arm means show higher divergence with AI, while the abstract, Results interpretation and Discussion describe lower divergence. Preserve all printed signs and labels pending an author correction (PDF pp. 1, 10, 13).

Individual semantic divergence: Methods specify pairwise distances within each person, while Results specify distances from a centroid. The participant-level paired description conflicts with t(364) in a study of 51 people. The actual independent-unit basis is unknown; se_basis and analysis-specific participant counts are null (PDF pp. 4, 7, 10).

Group semantic divergence: t(728) conflicts with a conventional independent-samples test on the stated 728-idea corpus. The implemented semantic-analysis sample and degrees of freedom need clarification; n_units is null because the corpus total is not a confirmed analysis count. This is explicitly an output-level test without reported participant adjustment (PDF pp. 5, 7, 10).

Semantic confidence intervals are not labelled as intervals for a raw difference or standardized effect. Subtraction order and the d standardizers are also unstated; ci_of and standardizer are null (PDF p. 10).
Paired-difference SDs, within-person correlations, paired difference SEs and the formulas for the reported unsigned r effects are not printed (PDF pp. 6, 8-9).

The whole-pool diversity indices, richness, exclusive categories and raw Existing Solutions totals have no printed inferential uncertainty. Category-size and uniqueness tests do not adjust for repeated outputs from each participant (PDF pp. 7, 9-10).
The category level used for the category-size comparison is unspecified (PDF pp. 7, 10).

Text-elaboration counting procedure, image-elaboration scorer and exact elaboration aggregation procedure are not specified. Participant-level coding follows the stated paired and sequence-group analyses and table counts; measure codes remain null (PDF pp. 6-9).
ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) is named, but no model release year, snapshot or experiment date is printed. ai_tool.year remains null (PDF p. 5).

Possible overlap with c201 / DOI 10.1002/cae.22817 is unconfirmed. The related paper is cited as prior work, not identified as a shared sample; shared_sample is null (PDF pp. 3, 13, 15; screening sample_overlap).

The paper does not report the six comparisons between Group B unaided in Task 2 and Group A unaided in Task 1. Those constructed after-AI estimates are excluded under extraction-spec.md rule 4; their original records remain in fixes[].old. The residual-learning discussion and order interactions do not supply those contrasts (PDF pp. 5-6, 8-9).
No supplement, appendix or public data/code link is identified in the complete document. Data availability states that data will be made available on request (PDF p. 15).
